\catchline

GLOBAL SOLUTIONS FOR THE ONE-DIMENSIONAL VLASOV–MAXWELL SYSTEM FOR LASER-PLASMA INTERACTION

JOSÉ A. CARRILLO Address: ICREA (Institució Catalana de Recerca i Estudis Avançats)
and Departament de Matemàtiques
Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona
08193 Bellaterra, Spain.
carrillo@mat.uab.es    SIMON LABRUNIE Address: Institut Élie Cartan (Mathématiques)
Université Henri Poincaré Nancy 1 et INRIA (projet CALVI)
54506 Vandœuvre-lès-Nancy, France.
labrunie@iecn.u-nancy.fr
Revised  (Day Month Year)
Abstract

We analyse a reduced 1D Vlasov–Maxwell system introduced recently in the physical literature for studying laser-plasma interaction. This system can be seen as a standard Vlasov equation in which the field is split in two terms: an electrostatic field obtained from Poisson’s equation and a vector potential term satisfying a nonlinear wave equation. Both nonlinearities in the Poisson and wave equations are due to the coupling with the Vlasov equation through the charge density. We show global existence of weak solutions in the non-relativistic case, and global existence of characteristic solutions in the quasi-relativistic case. Moreover, these solutions are uniquely characterised as fixed points of a certain operator. We also find a global energy functional for the system allowing us to obtain LpL^{p}-nonlinear stability of some particular equilibria in the periodic setting.

keywords
Kinetic equations; Vlasov–Maxwell system; existence and uniqueness of solutions; nonlinear stability.

The assumptions below the 1D model are the following: all variables depend on only one space variable, denoted xx, and the electrons are monokinetic in the directions transversal to xx. This is physically justifed by the fact that all the phenomena, especially heating, are much more rapid along the direction of propagation of the laser wave than in the transversal directions. So, the distribution function becomes:

𝔣⁡(t,𝐪,𝐩)=f⁡(t,x,px)​δ​(𝐩⊥−𝐩0​(t,x)).\mathfrak{f}(t,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p})=f(t,x,p_{x})\,\delta\left(\mathbf{p}_{\bot}-\mathbf{p}_{0}(t,x)\right). (7)

For a general polarisation, (9) would be duplicated, with a similar equation for AzA_{z}. Quadratic terms in AyA_{y} and AzA_{z} would be added in (12) as well as in the third term in (8). Let us notice that the model (8–13), as well as its extended version for a general polarisation, are classes of exact solutions to the relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell model, without any approximation. They are, as far as we know, the simplest exact solutions beyond 1D Vlasov–Poisson models.

1.1 Discussion of the relativistic character

The model (8–13) features a strongly non-linear coupling between the kinetic and electromagnetic variables, through the Lorentz factor (12). This phenomenon makes this system difficult to study on the theoretical level, but also to solve numerically: no splitting between the variables is possible.[16] This is why two reduced models have been defined by physicists:

  1. 1.

    The non-relativistic model (hereafter denoted NR) approximates the relativistic dynamic by the Newtonian one by setting γ=1\gamma=1 everywhere. It is physically justified when the temperature is low enough, so that the proportion of relativistic electrons is negligible, and the intensity of the pump wave is small.

  2. 2.

    The quasi-relativistic11 1 Also called semi-relativistic by some authors. model (QR) consists in approximating γ\gamma by 1+p2m2​c2\sqrt{1+\frac{p^{2}}{m^{2}\,c^{2}}} in the second term in (8) and in the definition of jj, and setting γ=1\gamma=1 in the third term in (8) and in the definition of nγn_{\gamma}, which amounts to setting nγ=nn_{\gamma}=n. It is acceptable when the proportion of ultra-relativistic (v≃cv\simeq c) electrons is negligible and the pump intensity is moderate.

The original model, with γ\gamma defined by (12) will be referred to as fully relativistic (FR). We remark that the NR model is a class of exact solutions to the non-relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system, i.e. (1–5) with 𝐯⁡(𝐩)=𝐩/m\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{p})=\mathbf{p}/m. By contrast, the QR model is only an approximation to the FR one. What makes its interest for the applied mathematician — besides its widespread use for simulation — is that it already contains certain features of higher-dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell systems, while being simpler to study.

x¯=ce​m​ε0n¯,t¯=x¯c,p¯=m​c;\overline{x}=\frac{c}{e}\,\sqrt{\frac{m\,{\varepsilon_{0}}}{\overline{n}}},\quad\overline{t}=\frac{\overline{x}}{c},\quad\overline{p}=m\,c\,;

E¯=m​c2​n¯ε0,A¯=m​ce,f¯=n¯m​c,ȷ¯=n¯​c.\overline{E}=\sqrt{\frac{m\,c^{2}\,\overline{n}}{{\varepsilon_{0}}}},\quad\overline{A}=\frac{m\,c}{e},\quad\overline{f}=\frac{\overline{n}}{m\,c},\quad\overline{\jmath}=\overline{n}\,c.

∂f∂t+pγ1​∂f∂x−(E+Aγ2​∂A∂x)​∂f∂p\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\frac{p}{\gamma_{1}}\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}-\left(E+\frac{A}{\gamma_{2}}\,\frac{\partial A}{\partial x}\right)\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial p} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (14)
∂E∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= j\displaystyle j (15)
∂2A∂t2−∂2A∂x2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}A}{\partial t^{2}}-\frac{\partial^{2}A}{\partial x^{2}} =\displaystyle= −nγ​A\displaystyle-n_{\gamma}\,A (16)

where the flux jj and the quasi-density nγn_{\gamma} are defined as

j⁡(t,x):=∫pγ1​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑p,nγ​(t,x):=∫1γ2​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑p.j(t,x):=\int\frac{p}{\gamma_{1}}\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p,\qquad n_{\gamma}(t,x):=\int\frac{1}{\gamma_{2}}\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p.

Of course, suitable initial conditions are supplied, namely

f⁡(0,x,p)=f0​(x,p),A⁡(0,x)=A0​(x),∂tA⁡(0,x)=A˙0​(x).f(0,x,p)=f_{0}(x,p),\ A(0,x)=A_{0}(x),\ \partial_{t}A(0,x)={\dot{A}}_{0}(x). (17)

For coherence, the initial electrostatic field must be given by:

E0(x)=E0(0)−∫0x(n0(y)−next(y))dy,where:n0(x):=∫f0(x,p)dp.E_{0}(x)=E_{0}(0)-\int_{0}^{x}\left(n_{0}(y)-n_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\right)\,\mathrm{d}y,\quad\mbox{where:}\quad n_{0}(x):=\int f_{0}(x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p.\ (18)

This guarantees that the Poisson (or Gauss) equation

∂E∂x=next−n,where:n(t,x):=∫f(t,x,p)dp,\frac{\partial E}{\partial x}=n_{\mathrm{ext}}-n,\quad\mbox{where:}\quad n(t,x):=\int f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p, (19)

will hold at any time provided the continuity equation is satisfied.

As far as the relativistic character of the particles is concerned, the three versions of the model are respectively:

  • •

    NR: γ1=γ2=1\gamma_{1}=\gamma_{2}=1.

  • •

    QR: γ1=1+p2,γ2=1\gamma_{1}=\sqrt{1+p^{2}},\ \gamma_{2}=1.

  • •

    FR: γ1=γ2=1+p2+A2\gamma_{1}=\gamma_{2}=\sqrt{1+p^{2}+A^{2}}.

Let us note that we shall investigate the existence of two classes of solutions for the system (14–16): periodic solutions, corresponding to initial data that are periodic in space, with a given period LL, and “open-space” solutions, i.e. solutions of finite mass and energy. In both cases, we always assume that nextn_{\mathrm{ext}} is at least bounded. Moreover, in the periodic setting, we assume that it is periodic and

∫0L(next​(x)−n0​(x))​𝑑x=0,\int_{0}^{L}\left(n_{\mathrm{ext}}(x)-n_{0}(x)\right)\,\mathrm{d}x=0,

so that E0E_{0} is indeed periodic.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first mathematical work on this particular Vlasov–Maxwell system (14–16): most of the previous mathematical works on reduced Vlasov–Maxwell models deal with systems living in two or one-and-a-half dimensions.[15, 14, 13, 2] In our case, the lower dimension is, to some extent, compensated by a stronger nonlinearity. This system shares some common features with the Nordström–Vlasov system recently studied in [7, 8]. Both systems present a Vlasov equation coupled to a wave equation whose right-hand side depends on the charge density. The main differences between them are the gravitational character of the Nordström–Vlasov system, our coupling with the Poisson equation and our more complicated right-hand side in the wave equation.

In this article, we shall only investigate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the NR and QR models. The differences between them can be bridged easily by using the shorthand notation

p^:=p​ (NR case),p^:=p1+p2​ (QR case).\widehat{p}:=p\mbox{ (NR case)},\quad\widehat{p}:=\frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^{2}}}\mbox{ (QR case)}.

On the other hand, the method presented in this article cannot apply directly to the FR model, because of its much stronger and more non-linear coupling between the kinetic and electromagnetic variables.

The next Section is devoted to reviewing some basic estimates for the Vlasov equation, and the different notions of solutions we will deal with. In Section 3 we use the procedure of [9] to prove the global existence of weak solutions in the NR and QR cases, which are characterised as unique fixed points of a certain operator.

This result is improved in two ways in Sections 4 and 5 respectively. We first prove the local-in-time existence of characteristic solutions in the NR case. The main difficulty in proving global existence of characteristic solutions consists in controlling the second space derivative of the vector potential AA or, equivalently, the first space derivative of the density nn. These difficulties are analogous to those found in the two and one-half dimensional Vlasov–Maxwell systems studied in [15, 14, 13, 2]. In the QR case, we obtain the existence result thanks to a good integral representation of the second derivative of AA reminiscent of similar ideas in [14], used recently in [8].

Finally, the last section is devoted to obtaining a global energy functional for the three cases. It is conserved in time by characteristic solutions in the NR and QR cases. This fact, together with now standard relative entropy arguments, leads to the LpL^{p}-nonlinear stability of a family of steady states in the periodic setting.

Whatever their regularity, we are mainly interested in global solutions, i.e. which exist for any time. However, our estimates will generally not be uniform in time and thus, we fix an arbitrary target time TT and we look for solutions defined on [0,T][0,T], for all T>0T>0. 2.1 The characteristic system

From now on, we denote

F⁡(t,x):=E⁡(t,x)+A⁡(t,x)​∂xA⁡(t,x)F(t,x):=E(t,x)+A(t,x)\,\partial_{x}A(t,x) (20)

the force generated by the fields (E,A)(E,A). The characteristic system associated to the transport equation (14) reads:

{d​Xd​s=P^​(s),d​Pd​s=−F⁡(s,X⁡(s)),X⁡(t)=x,P⁡(t)=p.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}X}{\mathrm{d}s}}=\widehat{P}(s),&{\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}s}}=-F(s,X(s)),\hfill\\ X(t)=x,&P(t)=p.\hfill\end{array}\right. (21)

E∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ)),A∈𝒞0​(0,T,W2,∞​(ℝ)).E\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right),\quad A\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right). (22)

From the uniqueness of the solution, we deduce a periodicity result:

Lemma 2.1.

If the force field is periodic in space, i.e.: ∀(t,x),F⁡(t,x+L)=F⁡(t,x)\forall(t,x),\ F(t,x+L)=F(t,x), then the following identity holds for all s,t,x,ps,\ t,\ x,\ p:

X⁡(s,t,x+L,p)=X⁡(s,t,x,p)+L,P⁡(s,t,x+L,p)=P⁡(s,t,x,p).X(s;t,x+L,p)=X(s;t,x,p)+L,\quad P(s;t,x+L,p)=P(s;t,x,p). (24)

The divergence of characteristics generated by different force fields is measured in a classical way (see for instance [9, Lemma 1] or [2] and references therein).

Proof 2.3.

Eq. (26) clearly stems from the integration of the equation for PP in (21). In the NR case, Eq. (25) immediately follows. In the QR case, we notice that

|dd​p​[p1+p2]|=1(1+p2)3/2≤1,\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\left[\frac{p}{\sqrt{1+p^{2}}}\right]\right|=\frac{1}{\left(1+p^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\leq 1,

so |P1^−P2^|≤|P1−P2|\left|\widehat{P^{1}}-\widehat{P^{2}}\right|\leq\left|{P^{1}}-{P^{2}}\right|, hence (25) by integration.

In a very similar fashion, the derivatives of the characteristics can be estimated in terms of derivatives of the force field.

Lemma 2.4.

The solution (X,P)(X,P) to (21), with F∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ))F\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right), is Lipschitz w.r.t. the variables (x,p)(x,p), and thus a.e. differentiable. The derivatives satisfy the following bound for a.e. (x,p)(x,p) and all 0≤τ≤t0\leq\tau\leq t:

max⁡{|∂X∂x​(τ)|,|∂X∂p​(τ)|,|∂P∂x​(τ)|,|∂P∂p​(τ)|}≤e(t−τ)​(1+‖∂xF‖t).\max\left\{\left|\frac{\partial X}{\partial x}(\tau)\right|,\ \left|\frac{\partial X}{\partial p}(\tau)\right|,\ \left|\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}(\tau)\right|,\ \left|\frac{\partial P}{\partial p}(\tau)\right|\right\}\leq\mathrm{e}^{(t-\tau)\,\left(1+\left\|\partial_{x}F\right\|_{t}\right)}. (27)
Proof 2.5.

Consider two final conditions (x1,p1)(x_{1},p_{1}) and (x2,p2)(x_{2},p_{2}). We use the shorthand:

(Xi(s),Pi(s)):=(X(s;t,xi,pi),P(s;t,xi,pi)),i=1, 2;\left(X_{i}(s),P_{i}(s)\right):=\left(X(s;t,x_{i},p_{i}),P(s;t,x_{i},p_{i})\right),\quad i=1,\ 2\,;

and we denote by Λ​F​(s)\Lambda F(s) the Lipschitz constant of F⁡(s,⋅)F(s,\cdot), i.e. supx|∂xF⁡(s,x)|\sup_{x}\left|\partial_{x}F(s,x)\right|.

By integrating the characteristic system (21), we get:

|X1​(τ)−X1​(τ)|+|P1​(τ)−P2​(τ)|\displaystyle\left|X_{1}(\tau)-X_{1}(\tau)\right|+\left|P_{1}(\tau)-P_{2}(\tau)\right|
≤|x1−x2|+|p1−p2|+∫τt{|P^1​(s)−P^2​(s)|+|F⁡(s,X1​(s))−F⁡(s,X2​(s))|}​𝑑s\displaystyle\mbox{}\;\leq|x_{1}-x_{2}|+|p_{1}-p_{2}|+\int_{\tau}^{t}\left\{\left|\widehat{P}_{1}(s)-\widehat{P}_{2}(s)\right|+\left|F(s,X_{1}(s))-F(s,X_{2}(s))\right|\right\}\,\mathrm{d}s
≤|x1−x2|+|p1−p2|+∫τt{|P1​(s)−P2​(s)|+Λ​F​(s)​|X1​(s)−X2​(s)|}​𝑑s\displaystyle\mbox{}\;\leq|x_{1}-x_{2}|+|p_{1}-p_{2}|+\int_{\tau}^{t}\left\{\left|P_{1}(s)-P_{2}(s)\right|+\Lambda F(s)\,\left|X_{1}(s)-X_{2}(s)\right|\right\}\,\mathrm{d}s
≤|x1−x2|+|p1−p2|+(1+‖∂xF‖t)​∫τt{|X1​(s)−X2​(s)|+|P1​(s)−P2​(s)|}​𝑑s.\displaystyle\mbox{}\;\leq|x_{1}-x_{2}|+|p_{1}-p_{2}|+\left(1+\left\|\partial_{x}F\right\|_{t}\right)\!\int_{\tau}^{t}\!\left\{\left|X_{1}(s)-X_{2}(s)\right|+\left|P_{1}(s)-P_{2}(s)\right|\right\}\,\mathrm{d}s.

Hence, by Gronwall’s lemma:

|X1​(τ)−X1​(τ)|+|P1​(τ)−P2​(τ)|≤(|x1−x2|+|p1−p2|)​e(t−τ)​(1+‖∂xF‖t),\left|X_{1}(\tau)-X_{1}(\tau)\right|+\left|P_{1}(\tau)-P_{2}(\tau)\right|\leq\left(|x_{1}-x_{2}|+|p_{1}-p_{2}|\right)\,\mathrm{e}^{(t-\tau)\,\left(1+\left\|\partial_{x}F\right\|_{t}\right)},

which proves the Lipschitz character of the functions X,PX,\ P and the quantitative estimate (27).

2.2 Characteristic, mild and weak solutions

In this work, we shall always assume the following two hypotheses about the initial distribution function f0f_{0}.

Hypothesis 1

In the open-space case, f0∈L1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}); in the periodic case,

f0∈LL1​(ℝ2)\displaystyle f_{0}\in L^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) :⁣=\displaystyle:= {f∈Lloc1(ℝ2):f(x+L,p)=f(x,p)a.e. in (x,p)∈ℝ2\displaystyle\biggl\{f\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}):\ f(x+L,p)=f(x,p)\,\mbox{a.e. in }(x,p)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
{ and f|(0,L)×ℝ∈L1((0,L)×ℝ)}.\displaystyle\hphantom{\biggl\lx@text@lbrace}\mbox{ and }\left.f\right|_{(0,L)\times{\mathbb{R}}}\in L^{1}((0,L)\times{\mathbb{R}})\biggr\}.

In both cases, (∂xf0,∂pf0)∈Lloc1​(ℝ2)(\partial_{x}f_{0},\partial_{p}f_{0})\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}).

Hypothesis 2

There exists a continuous, positive, even function g⁡(p)g(p), which moreover is decreasing in |p||p| and satisfies

∫ℝ|p|​g​(p)​𝑑p<∞,\int_{\mathbb{R}}|p|\,g(p)\,\mathrm{d}p<\infty,

such that

f0​(x,p)≤g⁡(p),|∂xf0​(x,p)|≤g⁡(p),|∂pf0​(x,p)|≤g⁡(p).f_{0}(x,p)\leq g(p),\quad\left|\partial_{x}f_{0}(x,p)\right|\leq g(p),\quad\left|\partial_{p}f_{0}(x,p)\right|\leq g(p).

Let us notice that these hypotheses imply, in the open-space case, that f0∈Wloc1,1​(ℝ2)∩W1,∞​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\cap W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}); the initial density n0∈L1​(ℝ)∩W1,∞​(ℝ)n_{0}\in L^{1}({\mathbb{R}})\cap W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}); and the initial electrostatic field, given by (11), E0∈W1,∞​(ℝ)E_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) if next∈L∞​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}), E0∈𝒞b1​(ℝ)E_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}) if next∈𝒞b0​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}). In the periodic case, one has similar properties in terms of periodic spaces; indeed, electrical neutrality ensures that n−nextn-n_{\mathrm{ext}} admits a periodic primitive.

For further reference, let us note that the function gr​(p)g_{r}(p) defined as

gr​(p)=g⁡(0)​ for ​|p|≤r,gr​(p)=g⁡(|p|−r)​ for ​|p|≥r,g_{r}(p)=g(0)\mbox{ for }|p|\leq r,\quad g_{r}(p)=g(|p|-r)\mbox{ for }|p|\geq r,

satisfies

∫ℝgr​(p)​𝑑p=2​r​g​(0)+∫ℝg⁡(p)​𝑑p.\int_{\mathbb{R}}g_{r}(p)\,\mathrm{d}p=2r\,g(0)+\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(p)\,\mathrm{d}p. (28)

The first notion of solutions which we consider is the one given by the usual characteristic method.

Definition 2.6.

Given a force field F∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ))F\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right) and f0f_{0} satisfying Hypotheses 1–2, we define the characteristic solution of the Vlasov equation (14) as:

f⁡(t,x,p):=f0​(X⁡(0,t,x,p),P⁡(0,t,x,p)),f(t,x,p):=f_{0}(X(0;t,x,p),P(0;t,x,p)), (29)

where (X⁡(s,t,x,p),P⁡(s,t,x,p))(X(s;t,x,p),P(s;t,x,p)) is the unique solution to (21). Moreover, assuming F∈𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b1​(ℝ))F\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right) and f0∈𝒞1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), then we shall often refer to the characteristic solution as a classical solution.

The previous definition gets clarified by the following result.

Lemma 2.7.

Under the assumption (22), the characteristic solution ff belongs to W1,∞​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ2))W^{1,\infty}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\right). If, moreover, f0∈𝒞1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) and (23) holds, then f∈𝒞1​(0,T,𝒞b1​(ℝ2))f\in{\cal C}^{1}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\right) and (14) is satisfied in the classical sense.

Proof 2.8.

According to classical dynamical system theory, (X⁡(s,t,x,p),P⁡(s,t,x,p))(X(s;t,x,p),P(s;t,x,p)) is 𝒞1{\cal C}^{1} w.r.t. ss, and also w.r.t. tt given the symmetry of these variables. The Lipschitz character in (x,p)(x,p) was obtained in Lemma 27. The first part of the conclusion then follows from Hypothesis 2, and the fact that the composition of Lipschitz functions is Lipschitz.

Moreover, under (23), the force is 𝒞1{\cal C}^{1}; as p↦p^p\mapsto\widehat{p} is 𝒞∞{\cal C}^{\infty}, we deduce that the solution to (21) is 𝒞1{\cal C}^{1}. The last statement then follows from the chain rule.

Mild solutions are introduced for relaxing the assumption of differentiability of the characteristics but keeping the fact that they define a family of Lipschitz homeomorphisms in phase space (see [1] and references therein). In fact, this definition can be rephrased using the concept of push-forward of a density through a map, which is quite well-known in mass transport theory.[18] The pushed-forward measure T#​ρT_{\#}\rho of a given measure ρ\rho in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} assigns mass

T#​ρ​[K]:=ρ⁡[T−1​(K)]T_{\#}\rho[K]:=\rho[T^{-1}(K)]

to each Borel set K⊂ℝnK\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. By this property, it satisfies that

∫ℝnψ​d​(T#​ρ)=∫ℝn(ψ∘T)​𝑑ρ\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\psi\,\mathrm{d}(T_{\#}\rho)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}(\psi\circ T)\,\mathrm{d}\rho

for all test functions ψ∈𝒞c0​(ℝn)\psi\in{\cal C}^{0}_{c}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}).

Definition 2.9.

Given a force field F∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ))F\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right) and f0∈Lloc1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), we say that a weakly continuous function f⁡(t,x,p)∈𝒞w​([0,T],Lloc1​(ℝ2))f(t,x,p)\in{\cal C}_{w}\left([0,T];L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\right) is a mild solution of the Vlasov equation (14) if it satisfies

∫ℝ2ψ⁡(x,p)​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p=∫ℝ2ψ⁡(X⁡(t,0,x,p),P⁡(t,0,x,p))​f0​(x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\psi(x,p)\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\psi(X(t;0,x,p),P(t;0,x,p))\,f_{0}(x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p (30)

for all test functions ψ∈𝒞c0​(ℝ2)\psi\in{\cal C}^{0}_{c}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}) and all t≥0t\geq 0, i.e.,

f⁡(t,x,p)=(X⁡(t,0,x,p),P⁡(t,0,x,p))#​f0f(t,x,p)=(X(t;0,x,p),P(t;0,x,p))_{\#}f_{0}

for all t≥0t\geq 0.

Taking into account the change of variables formula for Lipschitz functions,[11] we deduce that a characteristic solution is a mild solution of the Vlasov equation (14).

We can relax even more the assumptions on the force field and talk about distributional solutions for the Vlasov equation (14).

Definition 2.10.

Given a force field F∈L∞​((0,T)×ℝ)F\in L^{\infty}((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}) and f0∈Lloc1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), we say that f⁡(t,x,p)∈Lloc1​((0,T)×ℝ2)f(t,x,p)\in L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}) is a distributional solution of the Vlasov equation (14) if it satisfies

−∫0T∫ℝ2(∂ψ∂t+p^∂ψ∂x−F∂ψ∂p)fdxdpdt=∫ℝ2ψ(0,x,p)f0dxdp-\int_{0}^{T}\!\!\!\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\!\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}+\widehat{p}\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}-F\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial p}\right)\!f\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\,\mathrm{d}t\!=\!\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\psi(0,x,p)\,f_{0}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p (31)

for all test functions ψ∈𝒞c∞​([0,T)×ℝ2)\psi\in{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty}([0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}).

It is easy to check that any mild solution is a distributional solution. Moreover, in the particular case of characteristic solutions, in which f0∈W1,∞​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), ff belongs to W1,∞​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ2))W^{1,\infty}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\right) by Lemma 2.7. Therefore, one can check from the weak formulation (31) that ff satisfies the Vlasov equation (14) as an equality almost everywhere of locally bounded functions on (0,∞)×ℝ2(0,\infty)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.

2.3 A priori estimates

Since bounds for functions in 𝒞b1​(ℝ){\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}) or W1,∞​(ℝ)W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) can often be obtained in the same manner, we shall treat in the following the two types of characteristic solutions (classical and mild) together.

Thanks again to Hypothesis 2, one can define the density and flux:

{n,j}​(t,x):=∫ℝ{1,p^}​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑p.\{n,j\}(t,x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\{1,\widehat{p}\}\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p. (32)

Indeed, we have the following more general lemma for moments of characteristic solutions of (14). Let us denote by mk​(t,x)m_{k}(t,x) the moment of order k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} of a solution f⁡(t,x,p)f(t,x,p) with a given force field FF.

|mk​(t,x)|≤Mk+Rk​(M0+Mk,t​‖F‖t)\left|m_{k}(t,x)\right|\leq M_{k}+R_{k}\left(M_{0}+M_{k},t\left\|F\right\|_{t}\right) (33)

where Rk​(a,b)R_{k}(a,b) will be defined below. In particular, for k=0k=0 we obtain

‖n‖t≤M0+2​g​(0)​t​‖F‖t.\|n\|_{t}\leq M_{0}+2\,g(0)\,t\,\|F\|_{t}. (34)

From (29) and Hypothesis 2, we deduce:

|p|k​f​(t,x,p)≤|p|k​g​(|P⁡(0,t,x,p)|).|p|^{k}f(t,x,p)\leq|p|^{k}g\left(\left|P(0;t,x,p)\right|\right).

|mk​(t,x)|≤∫|p|k​gt​‖F‖t​(p)​𝑑p.\displaystyle\left|m_{k}(t,x)\right|\leq\int|p|^{k}g_{t\,\left\|F\right\|_{t}}(p)\,\mathrm{d}p.

∫ℝ|p|k​gr​(p)​𝑑p\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}|p|^{k}\,g_{r}(p)\,\mathrm{d}p =\displaystyle= 2​g​(0)k+1​rk+1+∑i=1kCki​rk−i​∫ℝ|p|i​g​(p)​𝑑p\displaystyle\frac{2\,g(0)}{k+1}\,r^{k+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{k}C_{k}^{i}\,r^{k-i}\,\int_{\mathbb{R}}|p|^{i}\,g(p)\,\mathrm{d}p (35)
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​g​(0)k+1​rk+1+(∑i=1kCki​rk−i)​∫ℝ(1+|p|k)​g​(p)​𝑑p\displaystyle\frac{2\,g(0)}{k+1}\,r^{k+1}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}C_{k}^{i}\,r^{k-i}\right)\,\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|p|^{k})\,g(p)\,\mathrm{d}p
≤\displaystyle\leq 2​g​(0)k+1​rk+1+(∑i=1kCki​rk−i)​(M0+Mk)\displaystyle\frac{2\,g(0)}{k+1}\,r^{k+1}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}C_{k}^{i}\,r^{k-i}\right)\,(M_{0}+M_{k})
:⁣=\displaystyle:= Rk​(M0+Mk,r).\displaystyle R_{k}(M_{0}+M_{k},r).

Finally, combining previous inequalities, we obtain (33). The estimate on the density (34) follows directly from previous arguments and (28) which defines the function R0R_{0}.

We can also estimate the divergence of moments corresponding to two different solutions of the Vlasov equation (14).

Lemma 2.13.

Let f1,f2f_{1},\ f_{2} be characteristic solutions of the Vlasov equation (14) with forces F1,F2∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ))F_{1},\ F_{2}\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right) respectively. Assume that the function g⁡(p)g(p) from Hypothesis 2 has the moment of order kk bounded, then

|m1,k−m2,k|​(t,x)≤Rk​(M0+Mk,maxi⁡‖Fi‖t)​∫0t‖F1−F2‖s​𝑑s.\left|m_{1,k}-m_{2,k}\right|(t,x)\leq R_{k}\left(M_{0}+M_{k},\max_{i}\left\|F_{i}\right\|_{t}\right)\,\int_{0}^{t}\left\|F_{1}-F_{2}\right\|_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s. (36)

+|∂f0∂p0(X02,P~)||P01−P02|}dp,\displaystyle+\left.\left|\frac{\partial f_{0}}{\partial p_{0}}\left(X^{2}_{0},\tilde{P}\right)\right|\,\left|P^{1}_{0}-P^{2}_{0}\right|\right\}\,\mathrm{d}p,

g⁡(|P~|)≤max⁡{g⁡(|P01|),g⁡(|P02|)}≤maxi⁡gt​‖Fi‖t​(p).g\left(|\tilde{P}|\right)\leq\max\left\{g\left(\left|P^{1}_{0}\right|\right),g\left(\left|P^{2}_{0}\right|\right)\right\}\leq\max_{i}g_{t\,\left\|F_{i}\right\|_{t}}(p).

A small variation on the above arguments allows us to prove that in fact, the density and flux are regular enough to satisfy the continuity equation. This is important in order to be able to say that the description via the Poisson equation (11) is equivalent to the Ampère equation (10).

Corollary 2.15.

Under Hypotheses 1–2 and the assumption (22), resp. (23), nn and jj are Lipschitz, resp. continuously differentiable in space and time and they satisfy

∂n∂t+∂j∂x=0.\frac{\partial n}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial j}{\partial x}=0. (38)

Moreover, there is a constant CC, depending only on the majorising function g⁡(p)g(p), such that:

‖∂n∂x‖t≤C​et⁡(1+‖∂xF‖t).\left\|\frac{\partial n}{\partial x}\right\|_{t}\leq C\,\mathrm{e}^{t\,\left(1+\left\|\partial_{x}F\right\|_{t}\right)}. (39)
Proof 2.16.

When the solution is classical, we can apply the chain rule and estimate directly the derivative in xx of the solution f⁡(t,x,p)f(t,x,p) to get

|∂f∂x|≤(supx|∂X∂x​(0)|)​|∂f0∂x0|+(supx|∂P∂x​(0)|)​|∂f0∂p0|.\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|\,\leq\,\left(\sup_{x}\left|\frac{\partial X}{\partial x}(0)\right|\right)\,\left|\frac{\partial f_{0}}{\partial x_{0}}\right|+\left(\sup_{x}\left|\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}(0)\right|\right)\,\left|\frac{\partial f_{0}}{\partial p_{0}}\right|.

Lemma 27 and Hypothesis 2 imply that (see previous Lemma):

|∂f∂x|≤et⁡(1+‖∂xF‖t)​gt​‖F‖t​(p),\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|\,\leq\,\mathrm{e}^{t\,\left(1+\left\|\partial_{x}F\right\|_{t}\right)}\,g_{t\,\|F\|_{t}}(p),

and thus ∂xf\partial_{x}f is integrable. Moreover, Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem implies that nn is Lipschitz or differentiable with respect to xx and hence (39). Similar arguments apply to ∂tn\partial_{t}n and ∂xj\partial_{x}j and the continuity equation (38) becomes an easy consequence of Eq. (14) upon integration on pp and using Hypotheses 1–2 on the initial data. In case the solution is only mild under assumption (22), one can reproduce the Lipschitz bounds by estimating the difference n⁡(t,x1)−n⁡(t,x2)n(t,x_{1})-n(t,x_{2}) using analogous arguments to previous Lemma 36, we leave the details to the reader.

And it stems from Lemma 24 that:

Lemma 2.17.

Under the hypotheses:

∀(x,p),f0​(x+L,p)=f0​(x,p);∀(t,x),{E,A}​(t,x+L)={E,A}​(t,x);\forall(x,p),\ f_{0}(x+L,p)=f_{0}(x,p)\,;\quad\forall(t,x),\ \{E,A\}(t,x+L)=\{E,A\}(t,x)\,;

there holds:

∀(t,x,p),f⁡(t,x+L,p)=f⁡(t,x,p),{n,j}​(t,x+L)={n,j}​(t,x).\forall(t,x,p),\ f(t,x+L,p)=f(t,x,p),\ \{n,j\}(t,x+L)=\{n,j\}(t,x).

Let us finally remark that thanks to the mass conservation property of the Vlasov equation, we estimate the integrals of nn. In the open-space case, we have

∫abn⁡(x)​𝑑x≤M,\int_{a}^{b}n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\leq M, (40)

where MM is the total mass of f0f_{0}. In the periodic case,

∫abn⁡(x)​𝑑x≤M⁡⌈b−aL⌉,\int_{a}^{b}n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\leq M\,\left\lceil\frac{b-a}{L}\right\rceil, (41)

where MM is now the mass of f0f_{0} over one period, and ⌈r⌉\lceil r\rceil is the smallest integer larger or equal to rr.

Moreover, in the open-space case we can estimate moments in xx under suitable additional assumptions on the initial data. In fact, let us consider the following

Hypothesis 3

f0​(x,p)≤g⁡(x)​g​(p)f_{0}(x,p)\leq g(x)\,g(p) in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.

By following the same lines of argument as in Lemma 34, we can prove:

Lemma 2.18.

Let ff be a characteristic solution of the Vlasov equation (14) in the open-space case with force field F∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ))F\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right) and assume that Hypothesis 3 is satisfied. Then, there exists a constant ZZ, depending polynomially on the first two moments of g⁡(p)g(p), tt and ‖F‖t\left\|F\right\|_{t}, such that

∫ℝ2(|x|+|p|)​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p≤Z⁡(M0,M1,t,‖F‖t).\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}(|x|+|p|)\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\leq Z\left(M_{0},M_{1},t,\left\|F\right\|_{t}\right). (42)

This can be generalised to all moments of ff and its derivatives, under

Hypothesis 4

|∂xf0​(x,p)|≤g⁡(x)​g​(p)\left|\partial_{x}f_{0}(x,p)\right|\leq g(x)\,g(p) and |∂pf0​(x,p)|≤g⁡(x)​g​(p)\left|\partial_{p}f_{0}(x,p)\right|\leq g(x)\,g(p) in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.

Lemma 2.19.

Assume that Hypotheses 3 and 4 hold, and that gg has its moment of order mm bounded. Then, for all k,ℓ≤mk,\ \ell\leq m, there exists a constant Zk,ℓZ_{k,\ell} such that, for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]:

∫∫⁡(|x|k+|p|ℓ)​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p\displaystyle\int\!\!\!\int\left(|x|^{k}+|p|^{\ell}\right)\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p ≤\displaystyle\leq Zk,ℓ,\displaystyle Z_{k,\ell},
∫∫⁡(|x|k+|p|ℓ)​|∂xf⁡(t,x,p)|​𝑑x​𝑑p\displaystyle\int\!\!\!\int\left(|x|^{k}+|p|^{\ell}\right)\,\left|\partial_{x}f(t,x,p)\right|\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p ≤\displaystyle\leq Zk,ℓ​et⁡(1+‖∂xF‖t),\displaystyle Z_{k,\ell}\,\mathrm{e}^{t\,\left(1+\|\partial_{x}F\|_{t}\right)},

and a similar bound holds for ∂pf\partial_{p}f.

3 Iterative procedure and global weak solutions

In this section, we present an iterative procedure to solve the 1D Vlasov–Maxwell system (14–16) for the NR and QR cases.

First, we define the iterative procedure based on the Cooper–Klimas[9] approach. Then, we will derive estimates on the fields that allow us to obtain a limit by telescopic series. However, these estimates will not allow us to get a global characteristic solution, due to the lack of a global-in-time estimate on the space derivative of the density, which is needed to control that of the right-hand side in (16), and thus the second space derivative of the vector potential. Therefore, at this level of generality we are only able to obtain global weak solutions. Improvements of this basic result, namely local (in the NR case) and global (in the QR case) existence of classical and mild solutions will be postponed to the next two sections.

We now fix an initial condition f0f_{0} for the distribution function, as well as initial data (A0,A˙0)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0}) for the vector potential. n0n_{0} and E0E_{0} are the density and electrostatic field given by f0f_{0}, as defined in (18). Let us remind that we always assume that the external density verifies next∈L∞​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}). We also fix a target time TT, and, if we are interested in periodic solutions, a space period LL.

3.1 Definition of the recurrence operator

Given the field pair (E,A)∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ)×W2,∞​(ℝ))(E,A)\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right), one constructs (E′,A′)=ℒ⁡(E,A)(E^{\prime},A^{\prime})={\cal L}(E,A) as follows.

  1. 1.

    The characteristic system (21) is solved, with the force FF given by (20).

  2. 2.

    One computes the characteristic solution to Vlasov’s equation by (29) and its density and flux (n,j)(n,j) by (32).

  3. 3.

    Finally, E′E^{\prime} and A′A^{\prime} are computed as:

    E′​(t,x)\displaystyle E^{\prime}(t,x) :⁣=\displaystyle:= E0​(x)+∫0tj⁡(s,x)​𝑑s,\displaystyle E_{0}(x)+\int_{0}^{t}j(s,x)\,\mathrm{d}s, (43)
    A′​(t,x)\displaystyle A^{\prime}(t,x) :⁣=\displaystyle:= 12{A0(x+t)+A0(x−t)+∫x−tx+tA˙0(y)dy\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\biggl\{A_{0}(x+t)+A_{0}(x-t)+\int_{x-t}^{x+t}{\dot{A}}_{0}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y (44)
    12{−∫0t∫x+s−tx+t−s(nA)(s,y)dyds}.\displaystyle\hphantom{\frac{1}{2}\,\biggl\lx@text@lbrace}\mbox{}-\int_{0}^{t}\int_{x+s-t}^{x+t-s}(n\,A)(s,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}s\biggr\}.

From Corollary 39 and the Duhamel formulae (90–92), we immediately deduce:

Theorem 3.1.

If (A0,A˙0)∈W2,∞​(ℝ)×W1,∞​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}), the operator ℒ{\cal L} maps 𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ)×W2,∞​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right) to itself. If (A0,A˙0)∈𝒞b2​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in{\cal C}^{2}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}), f0∈𝒞1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), and next∈𝒞b0​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}), then ℒ{\cal L} maps 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b1​(ℝ)×𝒞b2​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{2}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right) to itself.

Moreover, the Poisson equation (19) is satisfied for the pair (E′,n)(E^{\prime},n); and the time derivative of A′A^{\prime} is bounded in xx, i.e. A′∈𝒞1​(0,T,L∞​(ℝ))A^{\prime}\in{\cal C}^{1}\left(0,T;L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right) or 𝒞1​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{1}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right), even if AA does not belong a priori to such a space.

This ensures that the operator ℒ{\cal L} can be iterated. Of course, we shall need some quantitative estimates. To establish them is the goal of the next Subsection.

Moreover, we deduce from Lemma 2.17 the following

Corollary 3.2.

If (A0,A˙0)∈WL2,∞​(ℝ)×WL1,∞​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in W^{2,\infty}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{1,\infty}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}), the operator ℒ{\cal L} maps 𝒞0​(0,T,WL1,∞​(ℝ)×WL2,∞​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{2,\infty}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\right) to itself. If (A0,A˙0)∈𝒞L2​(ℝ)×𝒞L1​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in{\cal C}^{2}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}), f0∈𝒞L1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), and next∈𝒞L0​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in{\cal C}^{0}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}), then ℒ{\cal L} maps 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞L1​(ℝ)×𝒞L2​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{2}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\right) to itself.

3.2 A priori estimates

In the sequel, we shall always assume at least that (A0,A˙0)∈W2,∞​(ℝ)×W1,∞​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}). The constants denoted CC or CiC_{i} may vary from one line to the next, and depend on the initial conditions, TT and LL (but on nothing else).

First, we fix (E,A)∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ)×W2,∞​(ℝ))(E,A)\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right), and (E′,A′):=ℒ⁡(E,A)(E^{\prime},A^{\prime}):={\cal L}(E,A). FF is the force field corresponding to (E,A)(E,A).

For the electrostatic field we have the following properties:

Lemma 3.3.

The following estimates hold:

‖E′‖t\displaystyle\left\|E^{\prime}\right\|_{t} ≤\displaystyle\leq C0+C1​∫0t‖F‖s​𝑑s;\displaystyle C_{0}+C_{1}\,\int_{0}^{t}\|F\|_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\,; (45)

∂E′∂x=next−n,\frac{\partial E^{\prime}}{\partial x}=n_{\mathrm{ext}}-n,

For the vector potential, we have a similar result.

Lemma 3.5.

The following estimates hold:

‖A′‖t\displaystyle\left\|A^{\prime}\right\|_{t} ≤\displaystyle\leq C0+C1​∫0t‖A‖s​𝑑s,\displaystyle C_{0}+C_{1}\,\int_{0}^{t}\|A\|_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s, (47)

+C2​∫0t‖A2−A1‖s​𝑑s.\displaystyle\mbox{}+C_{2}\,\int_{0}^{t}\left\|A_{2}-A_{1}\right\|_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s.

3.3 Convergence of successive approximations

We start from the initial data (E0​(x),A0​(x))(E_{0}(x),A_{0}(x)), by extending them to constant-in-time functions over [0,T]×ℝ[0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}. Then, we construct a sequence (Ek,Ak)k∈ℕ(E_{k},A_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} by the recurrence formula:

(Ek+1,Ak+1):=ℒ⁡(Ek,Ak),∀k≥0.(E_{k+1},A_{k+1}):={\cal L}(E_{k},A_{k}),\quad\forall k\geq 0.

To establish the convergence of (Ek,Ak)k∈ℕ(E_{k},A_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}, the following result will be useful. It is easily proved by induction.

Lemma 3.11.

∀k∈ℕ,∀t∈[0,T],uk​(t)≤a​∑i=1k−1bi​tii!+c​bk​tkk!;\forall k\in{\mathbb{N}},\ \forall t\in[0,T],\quad u_{k}(t)\leq a\,\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{b^{i}\,t^{i}}{i!}+c\,\frac{b^{k}\,t^{k}}{k!}\;;

3.4 Global existence and properties of weak solutions

If (E,A)∈𝒞0​(0,T,W1,∞​(ℝ))×𝒞0​(0,T,W2,∞​(ℝ))(E,A)\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right)\times{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;W^{2,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right), then it is a fixed point of ℒ{\cal L} within this space. Thus, the triple (f,E,A)(f,E,A), where the function ff is defined by (29), is a characteristic solution to (14–19).

This fixed point and its associated characteristic solution, if they exist, are unique. Indeed, let (f1,E1,A1)(f_{1},E_{1},A_{1}) and (f2,E2,A2)(f_{2},E_{2},A_{2}) be two such solutions, with respective force fields F1F_{1} and F2F_{2}. Reasoning as in the proof of the above theorem shows:

‖A1−A2‖t+‖F1−F2‖t≤C​∫0t{‖A1−A2‖s+‖F1−F2‖s}​𝑑s;\left\|A_{1}-A_{2}\right\|_{t}+\left\|F_{1}-F_{2}\right\|_{t}\leq C\,\int_{0}^{t}\left\{\left\|A_{1}-A_{2}\right\|_{s}+\left\|F_{1}-F_{2}\right\|_{s}\right\}\,\mathrm{d}s\,;

hence A1=A2A_{1}=A_{2} and F1=F2F_{1}=F_{2} by Gronwall’s lemma, then E1=E2E_{1}=E_{2} by (50), and finally f1=f2f_{1}=f_{2} by the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem.

Without further a priori estimates on the second derivatives of the vector potential AA, we will not be able to obtain global existence of characteristic solutions. However, the bounds in Subsection 3.2 show that the norm of ℒ⁡(E,A){\cal L}(E,A) in 𝒞0​(0,T,L∞​(ℝ)×W1,∞​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right), resp. 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right), is controlled by the norm of (E,A)(E,A) in the same space. These considerations suggest to extend the operator ℒ{\cal L} to a bigger space in order to obtain weak solutions, which would also enjoy a uniqueness property. This programme cannot be achieved within the framework of 𝒞0​(0,T,L∞​(ℝ)×W1,∞​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\times W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}})\right). The reason is the well-known lack of density of smooth functions within L∞​(ℝ)L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) or W1,∞​(ℝ)W^{1,\infty}({\mathbb{R}}). But this obstruction is removed if one works within 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right).

Lemma 3.14.

Assume (A0,A˙0)∈𝒞b2​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in{\cal C}^{2}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}), f0∈𝒞1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), and next∈𝒞b0​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}). The operator ℒ{\cal L} can be extended to a continous operator from 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right) to itself, which satisfies the estimates of Subsection 3.2. If the initial conditions are periodic, then ℒ{\cal L} maps 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞L0​(ℝ)×𝒞L1​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\right) to itself.

Proof 3.15.

ℒ{\cal L} is defined on the dense subspace Y:=𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b1​(ℝ)×𝒞b2​(ℝ))Y:={\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{2}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right) of X:=𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ))X:={\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right), with values in XX. From (50, 51, 54), we see that it is uniformly continuous, in the norm of XX, on any set K∩YK\cap Y, where KK is a bounded set of XX. Hence, it admits a unique continuous extension from XX to itself.

The extension procedure preserves the estimates of Subsection 3.2, as their r.h.s. are uniformly continuous in the norm of XX on any K∩YK\cap Y. Finally, the closedness of 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞L0​(ℝ)×𝒞L1​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}})\right) within XX guarantees the invariance of this space by the extended operator.

Hence, the following theorem, whose proof rephrases that of Theorem 3.12.

Theorem 3.16.

Assume (A0,A˙0)∈𝒞b2​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ)(A_{0},{\dot{A}}_{0})\in{\cal C}^{2}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}), f0∈𝒞1​(ℝ2)f_{0}\in{\cal C}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), and next∈𝒞b0​(ℝ)n_{\mathrm{ext}}\in{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}). The operator ℒ{\cal L} admits a unique fixed point (E,A)∈𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)×𝒞b1​(ℝ))(E,A)\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right), which moreover belongs to 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b1​(ℝ))×𝒞1​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right)\times{\cal C}^{1}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right). Let us now check that this unique fixed point defines a distribution function ff in such a way that the triple (f,E,A)(f,E,A) is a global weak solution of the Vlasov–Maxwell system (14–19).

Theorem 3.17.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.16, let (Ek,Ak)k(E_{k},A_{k})_{k} a sequence converging to the fixed point (E,A)(E,A); without loss of generality, we can assume that its terms belong to 𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b1​(ℝ)×𝒞b2​(ℝ)){\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{1}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\times{\cal C}^{2}_{b}({\mathbb{R}})\right). Let (fk)k(f_{k})_{k} be the associated sequence of distribution functions obtained by the method of characteristics. Then, (fk)k(f_{k})_{k} converges uniformly in all its variables toward a function f∈𝒞0​(0,T,𝒞b0​(ℝ2))f\in{\cal C}^{0}\left(0,T;{\cal C}^{0}_{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\right), which does not depend on the sequence (Ek,Ak)k(E_{k},A_{k})_{k}, and the triple (f,E,A)(f,E,A) satisfies (14)–(19) in the sense of distributions.

Proof 3.18.

Repeating the argument of Lemma 36, we easily obtain the estimate

|fk​(t,x,p)−fℓ​(t,x,p)|≤(1+t)​maxi=k,ℓ​gt​‖Fi‖t​(p)​∫0t‖Fk−Fℓ‖s​𝑑s,\left|f_{k}(t,x,p)-f_{\ell}(t,x,p)\right|\leq(1+t)\,\max_{i=k,\ell}g_{t\,\left\|F_{i}\right\|_{t}}(p)\,\int_{0}^{t}\left\|F_{k}-F_{\ell}\right\|_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s, (59)

from which follows that (fk​(t))k\left(f_{k}(t)\right)_{k} is a Cauchy sequence in L∞L^{\infty} norm, uniformly in tt. A similar argument shows that, if we consider another approximating sequence denoted by tildes, fk​(t)−f~k​(t)f_{k}(t)-\tilde{f}_{k}(t) will converge to zero, uniformly in x,px,\ p and tt. Let us then call ff the common limit of all the sequences (fk)k\left(f_{k}\right)_{k}; its continuity in all variables follows from that of the fkf_{k}.

As fkf_{k} is a classical solution to the Vlasov equation, it is also a distributional solution, i.e. an equation similar to (31) holds, with ff and FF replaced resp. with fkf_{k} and FkF_{k}. For any test function ψ\psi, the integrals in this formula are taken over a compact subset of [0,T)×ℝ2[0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{2}. Thus, the uniform convergence in x,px,\ p and tt of the sequences (fk)k\left(f_{k}\right)_{k} and (Fk)k\left(F_{k}\right)_{k} ensures that (31) will also hold at the limit: the limiting triple (f,E,A)(f,E,A) satisfies (14–19) in the sense of distributions.

The above result can be improved in the following two ways. First, we show that f⁡(t)f(t) will retain the mass of the initial distribution f0f_{0}.

Proposition 3.19.

In the periodic case, fk​(t)f_{k}(t) converges toward f⁡(t)f(t) in LL1​(ℝ2)L^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), uniformly in tt, and the mass of f⁡(t)f(t) over one space period is equal to that of f0f_{0}. In the open-space case, under Hypothesis 3, fk​(t)f_{k}(t) converges weakly toward f⁡(t)f(t) in L1​(ℝ2)L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), and the mass of f⁡(t)f(t) is equal to that of f0f_{0}.

Inequality (59) shows that fk(t,x,⋅)f_{k}(t,x,\cdot) converges to f(t,x,⋅)f(t,x,\cdot) in L1​(ℝ)L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}), uniformly in xx and tt. Hence the convergence of fk​(t)f_{k}(t) toward f⁡(t)f(t) in L1​((a,b)×ℝ)L^{1}((a,b)\times{\mathbb{R}}) for any a<ba<b.

Yet, the fkf_{k} are classical solutions to the Vlasov equation. In the periodic case, they conserve the mass of f0f_{0} over one space period. So, f⁡(t)f(t) retains this mass.

In the open-space case, taking into account the L1L^{1} convergence in bounded intervals in space, it suffices to show that mass does not escape at infinity, uniformly in tt. Using Lemma 42, we obtain:

∫|x|+|p|>R|fk​(t,x,p)|​𝑑x​𝑑p≤1R​∫|x|+|p|>R(|x|+|p|)​fk​(t,x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p≤ZR→0,\int_{|x|+|p|>R}|f_{k}(t,x,p)|\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\leq\frac{1}{R}\,\int_{|x|+|p|>R}(|x|+|p|)\,f_{k}(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p\leq\frac{Z}{R}\to 0,

uniformly in kk and tt when R→∞R\to\infty. Thus, it is a standard argument to check that ∫ℝ2f⁡(t,x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p=limk∫ℝ2fk​(t,x,p)​𝑑x​𝑑p=M\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p=\lim_{k}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}f_{k}(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p=M.

The second useful precision is that f⁡(t)f(t) is “almost a mild solution” to (14).

Theorem 3.21.

The characteristics given by the FkF_{k} converge uniformly in all their variables toward a limit (X,P)(X,P), and Eq. (30) holds for this (X,P)(X,P) and f⁡(t)f(t) given by Theorem 3.17.

4 Local-in-time existence of characteristic solutions

In order to have stronger solutions, i.e. such that ff satisfies (14) in the characteristic sense, we need estimates on the Lipschitz constant of the force, which in turn amounts to bounding the second derivative of the vector potential. In this Section we show that, in both the NR and QR cases, the limiting vector potential given by Theorem 3.12 does satisfy such a bound, at least for a short time.

In the sequel, the operator ℒ{\cal L} will be that of Subsection 3.1. We no longer consider the extended version, so that we can obtain estimates based on characteristics.

Such a bound as (65) cannot be derived in the NR case, basically because the velocity p^=p\widehat{p}=p is not bounded: singularity formation could happen at any speed. The proof of the above two Lemmas does not apply, because neither 1/(p−1)1/(p-1) nor its derivative −1/(p−1)2-1/(p-1)^{2} are locally integrable near p=1p=1, and the integrations by parts would be unjustified.

Nevertheless, in the QR case we immediately deduce the following theorem:

Theorem 5.5.

Let (Ek,Ak)k∈ℕ(E_{k},A_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} and (E,A)(E,A) be as in Theorem 3.12. The sequence (∂x2Ak)k∈ℕ\left(\partial_{x}^{2}A_{k}\right)_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} converges uniformly in xx and tt. As a consequence, the triple (f,E,A)(f,E,A) defines a characteristic solution to (14–16) on the interval [0,T]\left[0,T\right].

Proof 5.6.

The convergence of (∂x2Ak)k∈ℕ\left(\partial_{x}^{2}A_{k}\right)_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} immediately follows from (65) and the convergence results of Theorem 3.12, and the limit is necessarily equal to ∂x2A\partial_{x}^{2}A. So, ∂xFk\partial_{x}F_{k} converges uniformly towards the xx-derivative of the force given by (E,A)(E,A); and we get the conclusion.

6 Stability of equilibria

In this section, we restrict ourselves to classical solutions to the system (14–19). Thus, in the NR case, we take T>0T>0 small enough to have a classical solution on [0,T][0,T].

Furthermore, we only consider solutions of finite mass, energy and entropy — the latter concepts being precised in the following Subsection — in order to rule out some unphysical or pathological behaviours.

6.1 Energies and entropy for the system (14–19)

The physical energy of the system naturally splits in two parts, the transversal energy made up of the terms containing the vector potential AA, and the longitudinal energy for the other terms.

The transversal energy is written W​T​[f⁡(t),A⁡(t),∂tA⁡(t)]WT[f(t),A(t),\partial_{t}A(t)], where:

W​T​[f,A,A˙]:=12​∫{n⁡[f]​(x)​A​(x)2+|∂xA⁡(x)|2+A˙​(x)2}​𝑑xWT[f,A,{\dot{A}}]:=\frac{1}{2}\,\int\left\{n[f](x)\,A(x)^{2}+\left|{\partial_{x}A}(x)\right|^{2}+{\dot{A}}(x)^{2}\right\}\,\mathrm{d}x (66)

and, of course, n⁡[f]n[f] denotes the density of ff. In the periodic case, the integral is to be taken over one space period; in the open-space case, over the whole space.

Let 𝒱=H1​(ℝ){\cal V}=H^{1}({\mathbb{R}}) or HL1​(ℝ)H^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}) and ℋ=L2​(ℝ){\cal H}=L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}) or LL2​(ℝ)L^{2}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}). dd​t​W​T​[f⁡(t),A⁡(t),∂tA⁡(t)]=12​∫∂tn⁡(t,x)​A​(t,x)2​𝑑x.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}WT[f(t),A(t),\partial_{t}A(t)]=\frac{1}{2}\,\int\partial_{t}n(t,x)\,A(t,x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x. (67)

dd​t​12​(‖∂A∂t‖2+‖∂A∂x‖2)=−(n⁡(t)​A​(t)|∂A∂t),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\frac{1}{2}\,\left(\left\|\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}\right\|^{2}+\left\|\frac{\partial A}{\partial x}\right\|^{2}\right)=-\left(n(t)\,A(t)\Bigm|\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}\right),

We now study the longitudinal energy. To this end, we first define the electrostatic field and potential functionals. In the open-space case, we set

E[f]=−∂xΦ[f]:=∂x(ϕext−ϕ[f]),E[f]=-\partial_{x}\Phi[f]:=\partial_{x}\left(\phi_{\mathrm{ext}}-\phi[f]\right),

due to Lemma 42. We remark that ϕ\phi is a linear, self-adjoint and positive operator. As for the potential ϕext\phi_{\mathrm{ext}}, we assume that it satisfies the following hypotheses.

Definition 6.3.

while in the open-space case, one sets:

However, in the open-space case |∂xϕ⁡[f]|2|\partial_{x}\phi[f]|^{2} is clearly not integrable and the integration by parts to arrive to a formula like (73) are not justified. We will comment on this in the next subsection.

Now, we can analyse the evolution of the longitudinal energy.

Proposition 6.4.

Let (f,E,A)(f,E,A) be a classical solution to (14–19). Assume Hypotheses 1, 2 and 7 if the system is NR, Hypotheses 1, 2 and 5 if it is QR. From (67), (75) and the continuity equation (38), we immediately deduce:

Theorem 6.6.

Under the hypotheses of Propositions 67 and 75, the energy W⁡(t):=W​T​[f⁡(t),A⁡(t),∂tA⁡(t)]+W​L​[f⁡(t)]W(t):=WT\left[f(t),A(t),\partial_{t}A(t)\right]+WL[f(t)] is constant.

For reference, we give the formulae for the energy in the FR case. There is no splitting in transversal and longitudinal parts. The total energy is given by:

W⁡(t)\displaystyle W(t) :⁣=\displaystyle:= ∫0L∫[1+p2+A​(t,x)2−12​Φ​[f⁡(t)]​(x)]​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑p​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{0}^{L}\!\int\left[\sqrt{1+p^{2}+A(t,x)^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\,\Phi[f(t)](x)\right]\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p\,\mathrm{d}x (79)
+12​∫0L[|∂A∂t​(t,x)|2+|∂A∂x​(t,x)|2]​𝑑x\displaystyle\mbox{}+\frac{1}{2}\,\int_{0}^{L}\left[\left|\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}(t,x)\right|^{2}+\left|\frac{\partial A}{\partial x}(t,x)\right|^{2}\right]\,\mathrm{d}x

in the periodic case, and

W⁡(t)\displaystyle W(t) :⁣=\displaystyle:= ∫ℝ∫[1+p2+A​(t,x)2+ϕext​(x)−12​ϕ​[f⁡(t)]​(x)]​f​(t,x,p)​𝑑p​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int\left[\sqrt{1+p^{2}+A(t,x)^{2}}+\phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\,\phi[f(t)](x)\right]\,f(t,x,p)\,\mathrm{d}p\,\mathrm{d}x (80)
+12​∫ℝ[|∂A∂t​(t,x)|2+|∂A∂x​(t,x)|2]​𝑑x\displaystyle\mbox{}+\frac{1}{2}\,\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[\left|\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}(t,x)\right|^{2}+\left|\frac{\partial A}{\partial x}(t,x)\right|^{2}\right]\,\mathrm{d}x

in the open-space case. The reader may check that these expressions are formally constant, even though the mere existence of classical solutions is an open problem, and subtler arguments are probably necessary to justify the calculations.

Definition 6.7.

Let σ∈𝒞2((0,+∞))∩𝒞0([0,+∞))\sigma\in{\cal C}^{2}((0,+\infty))\cap{\cal C}^{0}([0,+\infty)) be a strictly convex and bounded-from-below function, which satisfies

lims→+∞σ⁡(s)s=+∞.\lim_{s\to+\infty}\frac{\sigma(s)}{s}=+\infty.

Let γ\gamma denote the generalised inverse of −σ′-\sigma^{\prime} (extended by 0 if necessary): it is a decreasing function in its support.

The entropy associated to a distribution function ff is defined as:

Sσ​[f]:=∫∫⁡σ⁡(f⁡(x,p))​𝑑p​𝑑x.S_{\sigma}[f]:=\int\!\!\!\int\sigma(f(x,p))\,\mathrm{d}p\,\mathrm{d}x.

The most classical example is σ⁡(s)=s​ln⁡s−s\sigma(s)=s\,\ln s-s, i.e. γ⁡(s)=e−s\gamma(s)=\mathrm{e}^{-s}, associated to Maxwellian distribution functions.

Clearly, SσS_{\sigma} is a convex, bounded-from-below, weakly lower semicontinuous functional on its domain of definition. From [5], we know that for any f∗∈L1​(ℝd)f_{*}\in L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{d}), there exists a function σ\sigma as above s.t. Sσ​[f∗]S_{\sigma}[f_{*}] is finite. Thus, we shall choose σ\sigma according to the following

Hypothesis 8

In the periodic case, ∫σ⁡(g⁡(p))​𝑑p<∞\int\sigma(g(p))\,\mathrm{d}p<\infty. In the open-space case, ∫σ⁡(g⁡(0)​g​(p))​𝑑p<∞\int\sigma(g(0)\,g(p))\,\mathrm{d}p<\infty and ∫∫⁡σ⁡(g⁡(x)​g​(p))​𝑑x​𝑑p<∞\int\!\!\!\int\sigma(g(x)\,g(p))\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p<\infty.

In this case, the following identities hold:

∫σ​(gr​(p))​𝑑p\displaystyle\int\sigma\left(g_{r}(p)\right)\,\mathrm{d}p =\displaystyle= 2​r​σ​(g⁡(0))+∫σ⁡(g⁡(p))​𝑑p;\displaystyle 2\,r\,\sigma(g(0))+\int\sigma(g(p))\,\mathrm{d}p\,;
∫∫⁡σ⁡(gρ​(x)​gr​(p))​𝑑x​𝑑p\displaystyle\int\!\!\!\int\sigma\left(g_{\rho}(x)\,g_{r}(p)\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p =\displaystyle= 4​ρ​r​g​(0)+2​(ρ+r)​∫σ⁡(g⁡(0)​g​(s))​𝑑s\displaystyle 4\,\rho\,r\,g(0)+2\,(\rho+r)\,\int\sigma(g(0)\,g(s))\,\mathrm{d}s
+∫∫⁡σ⁡(g⁡(x)​g​(p))​𝑑x​𝑑p.\displaystyle\mbox{}+\int\!\!\!\int\sigma(g(x)\,g(p))\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p.

Then, the finiteness and differentiability of Sσ​[f​(t)]S_{\sigma}[f(t)] stem from arguments very similar to the proof of Proposition 75, and one can easily deduce.

Theorem 6.8.

Under Hypothesis 8, the function Sσ​[f​(t)]S_{\sigma}[f(t)] is constant on [0,T][0,T].

6.2 Equilibria of (14–19)

We are looking for solutions to (14–19) which do not depend on time, i.e., solutions to the coupled problem in (f⁡(x,p),A⁡(x))(f(x,p),A(x)):

p^​∂f∂x+dd​x​[Φ⁡[f]−A22]​∂f∂p\displaystyle\widehat{p}\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left[\Phi[f]-\frac{A^{2}}{2}\right]\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial p} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (81)
−d2​Ad​x2+n⁡[f]​A\displaystyle-\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}A}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}+n[f]\,A =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 (82)

with the potential satisfying the Poisson equation −∂2∂x2​Φ​[f]=next−n⁡[f]-\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x^{2}}\Phi[f]=n_{\mathrm{ext}}-n[f].

We have the following result

Lemma 6.9.

Any classical solution to (81–82) s.t. M>0M>0 and A∈𝒱A\in{\cal V} is a Vlasov–Poisson equilibrium, i.e. it has the form (f∞,0)(f_{\infty},0), where f∞f_{\infty} solves

p^​∂f∞∂x+d​Φ​[f∞]d​x​∂f∞∂p=0,\widehat{p}\,\frac{\partial f_{\infty}}{\partial x}+\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi[f_{\infty}]}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\frac{\partial f_{\infty}}{\partial p}=0, (83)

with −∂2∂x2​Φ​[f∞]=next−n⁡[f∞]-\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x^{2}}\Phi[f_{\infty}]=n_{\mathrm{ext}}-n[f_{\infty}] and consequently satisfies:

f∞​(x,p)=ℱ⁡(κ⁡(p)−Φ⁡[f∞]​(x)),f_{\infty}(x,p)={\cal F}\left(\kappa(p)-\Phi[f_{\infty}](x)\right), (84)

for some function ℱ{\cal F}.

Proof 6.10.

If A∈𝒱A\in{\cal V}, then for any B∈𝒱B\in{\cal V},

af​(A,B):=∫(A′​(x)​B′​(x)+n⁡[f]​(x)​A​(x)​B​(x))​𝑑x=0.a_{f}(A,B):=\int\left(A^{\prime}(x)\,B^{\prime}(x)+n[f](x)\,A(x)\,B(x)\right)\,\mathrm{d}x=0. (85)

Now, take B=AB=A to deduce that af​(A,A)=0a_{f}(A,A)=0. Since both terms in af​(A,A)a_{f}(A,A) are non-negative, we deduce that

∫|A′​(x)|2​𝑑x=∫n⁡[f]​(x)​A​(x)2​𝑑x=0.\int|A^{\prime}(x)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\int n[f](x)\,A(x)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=0.

From the first identity we conclude AA is constant, while from the second we conclude A=0A=0 since n⁡[f]>0n[f]>0 on some non-negligible subset of ℝ{\mathbb{R}} or (0,L)(0,L). We are left with (83), whose solution is well-known to be of the form (84).

The function ℱ{\cal F} can be precised by demanding that the solution should minimise a “free energy” functional. In other words, the choice of the entropy function σ\sigma is determined by the particular equilibrium one is interested in.

Definition 6.11.

Let f∈L1​(ℝ2)f\in L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), resp. f∈LL1​(ℝ2)f\in L^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}), the free energy of ff is:

Kσ​[f]:=W​L​[f]+Sσ​[f].K_{\sigma}[f]:=WL[f]+S_{\sigma}[f].

Let then A∈𝒱A\in{\cal V} and A˙∈ℋ{\dot{A}}\in{\cal H}; we set

K​Tσ​[f,A,A˙]:=Kσ​[f]+W​T​[f,A,A˙].KT_{\sigma}[f,A,{\dot{A}}]:=K_{\sigma}[f]+WT[f,A,{\dot{A}}].

We consider the set of suitable distribution functions with fixed mass, i.e.

𝒦⁡(L,M):={f∈LL1​(ℝ2):f≥0​ a.e. and ​‖f‖LL1​(ℝ2)=M}.{\cal K}(L,M):=\left\{f\in L^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}):f\geq 0\mbox{ a.e. and }\|f\|_{L^{1}_{L}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})}=M\right\}.
Lemma 6.12.

In the periodic case, K​TσKT_{\sigma} is a strictly convex and bounded-from-below functional on 𝒦⁡(L,M)×𝒱×ℋ{\cal K}(L,M)\times{\cal V}\times{\cal H}. It has a unique global minimum which takes the form (f∞,σ,0,0)\left(f_{\infty,\sigma},0,0\right), where

f∞,σ=γ⁡(κ⁡(p)−Φ⁡[f∞,σ]​(x)−α)f_{\infty,\sigma}=\gamma\left(\kappa(p)-\Phi[f_{\infty,\sigma}](x)-\alpha\right) (86)

and is therefore a stationary solution of the Vlasov–Poisson system. The constant α\alpha is uniquely determined by MM and LL.

Proof 6.13.

Eq. (72) shows that W​LWL is convex in this case; it is clearly lower semicontinuous and on 𝒦⁡(L,M){\cal K}(L,M) it is bounded from below. Since SσS_{\sigma} enjoys the same property and is strictly convex, we deduce that KσK_{\sigma} has a unique global minimum f∞,σf_{\infty,\sigma}. Writing the Lagrange equation expressing the minimisation under the constraint ∫f=M\int f=M (cf. [3, 5]), yields the formula (86), where α\alpha is the Lagrange multiplier. Then, it is clear that for any (f,A,A˙)≠(f∞,σ,0,0)(f,A,{\dot{A}})\neq(f_{\infty,\sigma},0,0),

K​Tσ​[f,A,A˙]>K​Tσ​[f,0,0]>K​Tσ​[f∞,σ,0,0],KT_{\sigma}[f,A,{\dot{A}}]>KT_{\sigma}[f,0,0]>KT_{\sigma}\left[f_{\infty,\sigma},0,0\right],

where the last inequality is a consequence of the results in [3, 5].

A similar result in the open-space case does not hold in our case, in contrast to the situation studied for nonlinear stability of the Vlasov–Poisson system in higher dimensions. [17, 4, 3, 5] The main difference in 1D being that ∂xϕ⁡[f]∉L2​(ℝ)\partial_{x}\phi[f]\notin L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}) as pointed out before. Sobolev embeddings in d≥2d\geq 2 allow, under confining conditions on the external potential ϕext\phi_{\mathrm{ext}}, to deduce a result similar to previous Lemma. [10, 3, 5] Moreover, the functional K​TσKT_{\sigma} ceases to be convex in our 1D open-space case.

6.3 LpL^{p}-nonlinear stability of equilibria in the periodic case

In this subsection, we just collect the known results in several references and applied to the particular case we deal with. Like in [17, 4, 5], one can rewrite:

K​Tσ​[f,A,A˙]−K​Tσ​[f∞,σ,0,0]=Σσ​[f|f∞,σ]+W​T​[f,A,A˙],KT_{\sigma}[f,A,{\dot{A}}]-KT_{\sigma}\left[f_{\infty,\sigma},0,0\right]=\Sigma_{\sigma}\left[f|f_{\infty,\sigma}\right]+WT[f,A,{\dot{A}}], (87)

where the relative entropy of the distribution function ff w.r.t. gg is defined as:

Σσ​[f|g]:=∫∫⁡[σ⁡(f)−σ⁡(g)−σ′​(g)​(f−g)]​𝑑x​𝑑p+12​∫|∂xΦ⁡[f−g]|2​𝑑x.\qquad\Sigma_{\sigma}[f|g]:=\int\!\!\!\int[\sigma(f)-\sigma(g)-\sigma^{\prime}(g)(f-g)]\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}p+\frac{1}{2}\int\left|\partial_{x}\Phi[f-g]\right|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x. (88)

Yet, as a consequence of Theorems 6.6 and 6.8, K​Tσ​[f⁡(t),A⁡(t),∂tA⁡(t)]KT_{\sigma}\left[f(t),A(t),\partial_{t}A(t)\right] is constant for any classical solution to (14–19). This implies (see [17, 4, 5]) that:

  1. 1.

    The LpL^{p} norm of f−f∞,σf-f_{\infty,\sigma} is bounded for 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq 2, if infσ′′​(s)/sp−2>0\inf\sigma^{\prime\prime}(s)/s^{p-2}>0.

  2. 2.

    The L2L^{2} norm of f−f∞,σf-f_{\infty,\sigma} is bounded, if f∞,σf_{\infty,\sigma} is a Maxwellian, i.e. σ⁡(s)=s​ln⁡s−s\sigma(s)=s\,\ln s-s.

  3. 3.

    The H1H^{1} norm of Φ⁡[f]−Φ⁡[f∞,σ]\Phi[f]-\Phi[f_{\infty,\sigma}] is bounded.

  4. 4.

    The transversal energy is bounded — indeed, we already knew this, and even a little bit more, from Proposition 67.

Here, all the norms are taken for x∈[0,L]x\in[0,L], p∈ℝp\in{\mathbb{R}}.

The first three points follow from §§3 and 4 of [5] and references therein. Indeed, the arguments in these passages are independent of the dimension.

In other words, the one-dimensional periodic Vlasov–Poisson equilibria are LpL^{p}-nonlinearly stable under one-dimensional Vlasov–Maxwell perturbations.

Let us finally mention that Landau damping was proved in [6] in the case of the Vlasov–Poisson system in the periodic case. As a consequence, it was proved in [6] that some Vlasov–Poisson equilibria which are L1L^{1}-nonlinearly stable, are unstable for a weak topology. This is not known to happen in our 1D Vlasov–Maxwell system, although numerical computations seem to indicate that nonlinear Landau damping should occur in this model. Let us point out that there is no contradiction between these two stability assertions, since weak topology neighbourhoods of the equilibria are much larger than L1L^{1} neighbourhoods.

Appendix B Convergence of the sequence defined by (62)

Here is the technical lemma announced in the proof of Theorem 4.3.

Lemma B.1.

Let (vk​(t))k∈ℕ(v_{k}(t))_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} and φt\varphi_{t} be defined by (62).

  1. 1.

    There exists T1<+∞T_{1}<+\infty such that, for 0<t<T10<t<T_{1}, φt\varphi_{t} admits two fixed points vt<vtv_{t}<v^{t}. If v0​(t)<vtv_{0}(t)<v^{t}, the unstable fixed point, then the sequence vk​(t)v_{k}(t) converges toward the stable point vtv_{t}.

  2. 2.

    For t>T1t>T_{1}, there is no fixed point, and (vk​(t))k∈ℕ(v_{k}(t))_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} diverges to +∞+\infty.

  3. 3.

    When tt tends to zero, vtv^{t} goes to infinity, while vtv_{t} remains bounded.

Consequently, there exists 0<T∗≤T10<T^{*}\leq T_{1} s.t. (vk​(t))k∈ℕ(v_{k}(t))_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} is convergent for 0≤t<T∗0\leq t<T^{*}.

Proof B.2.

As φt\varphi_{t} is convex and increasing, there are only three possibilities:

  1. 1.

    The equation φt​(x)=x\varphi_{t}(x)=x admits two solutions vt<vtv_{t}<v^{t}, which are respectively stable and unstable fixed points: 0<φt′​(vt)<10<\varphi^{\prime}_{t}(v_{t})<1 and φt′​(vt)>1\varphi^{\prime}_{t}(v^{t})>1.

  2. 2.

    The two solutions merge in a unique fixed point vv, which satifies both φt​(v)=v\varphi_{t}(v)=v and φt′​(v)=1\varphi^{\prime}_{t}(v)=1; it is stable on the left side, unstable on the right side.

  3. 3.

    There is no fixed point at all, and φt​(x)>x\varphi_{t}(x)>x for all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}.

The case 1 is achieved for tt small enough. Indeed:

limt→0β​t​et⁡(1+x)=0,∀x∈ℝ+.\lim_{t\to 0}\beta\,t\,\mathrm{e}^{t\,(1+x)}=0,\quad\forall x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{+}.

Hence, for any μ>1\mu>1, there exists tμ>0t_{\mu}>0 s.t. φt​(μ​α)<μ​α\varphi_{t}(\mu\,\alpha)<\mu\,\alpha for t<tμt<t_{\mu}. On the other hand, φt​(α)>α\varphi_{t}(\alpha)>\alpha. Hence, φt\varphi_{t} has (at least) one fixed point in the interval (α,μ​α)(\alpha,\mu\,\alpha) when t<tμt<t_{\mu}. Given that φt​(x)≫x\varphi_{t}(x)\gg x when x→+∞x\to+\infty, there is another fixed point in (μ​α,+∞)(\mu\,\alpha,+\infty).

Then, we notice that, when xx is fixed, φt​(x)\varphi_{t}(x) is a decreasing function of tt. This has two consequences. Firstly, if s<ts<t and φt\varphi_{t} has fixed points, then φs\varphi_{s} also has fixed points. This proves the existence of T1T_{1}, which may be finite or not. Clearly, if T1T_{1} is finite, it achieves the case 2. Eliminating vv between φt​(v)=v\varphi_{t}(v)=v and φt′​(v)=1\varphi^{\prime}_{t}(v)=1 gives the following equation for tt:

β​t2​eα​t2+2​t=1.\beta\,t^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{\alpha\,t^{2}+2\,t}=1.

As the l.h.s. is zero for t=0t=0, infinite for t=+∞t=+\infty and strictly increasing in tt, the equation admits a unique solution T1∈(0,+∞)T_{1}\in(0,+\infty).

The behaviour of vk+1​(t)=φt​(vk​(t))v_{k+1}(t)=\varphi_{t}(v_{k}(t)) then follows from the elementary theory of sequences (Figure 1), and the claims 1 and 2 are obtained.

The second consequence is that vtv_{t} and vtv^{t} are resp. decreasing and increasing functions of tt. Hence, vtv_{t} is bounded when t→0t\to 0. On the other hand, vt>xtv^{t}>x^{t}, where xtx^{t} is defined by φt′​(xt)=1\varphi^{\prime}_{t}(x^{t})=1. The latter equation gives

β​t2​et⁡(1+xt)=1⇔xt=1t​ln⁡(1β​t2)−1→+∞when ​t→0.\beta\,t^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{t\,(1+x^{t})}=1\iff x^{t}=\frac{1}{t}\,\ln\left(\frac{1}{\beta\,t^{2}}\right)-1\to+\infty\quad\mbox{when }t\to 0.

This proves the third claim. Finally, let us remark that v0​(t)v_{0}(t) is indeed independent of tt: E0E_{0} and A0A_{0}, hence F0F_{0} are constant in time. Consequently, for tt small enough, vt>v0​(t)v^{t}>v_{0}(t). This gives the last part of the conclusion.
